assets.prompt: Exact text-free scientific diagram: Three solid layers sit above one another; a bracket groups the thin top layer and the layer beneath it.
assets.alt: Three solid layers sit above one another; a bracket groups the thin top layer and the layer beneath it.
assets.caption: The bracket groups crust (thin brown top) and rigid uppermost mantle (gray) into lithosphere, the material of a tectonic plate. The tan region represents warmer, mostly solid mantle that can deform slowly. Thicknesses are not to scale.

assets.prompt: Exact text-free scientific diagram: Two brown plates separate above tan rock while an orange wedge and upward arrow mark rising magma.
assets.alt: Two brown plates separate above tan rock while an orange wedge and upward arrow mark rising magma.
assets.caption: Divergent boundary, side view: plates move apart. At an ocean ridge, rising mantle partly melts and magma forms new oceanic crust. Most mantle is solid; the orange wedge is local magma. Not to scale.

assets.prompt: Exact text-free scientific diagram: Inward arrows push two continental blocks toward a folded mountain belt with thickened rock below.
assets.alt: Inward arrows push two continental blocks toward a folded mountain belt with thickened rock below.
assets.caption: Continental collision thickens and folds crust, helping build the Himalayas. This is a convergent boundary, but it differs from oceanic subduction. Mountains are not automatically volcanoes.

assets.prompt: Exact text-free scientific diagram: Two blocks on either side of a straight fault have arrows pointing in opposite directions parallel to the fault.
assets.alt: Two blocks on either side of a straight fault have arrows pointing in opposite directions parallel to the fault.
assets.caption: Transform boundary, map view: plates slide past along their shared boundary. Locked patches can store stress and later slip in earthquakes; some parts creep. This is a motion model, not a map of the San Andreas Fault.
